question: What if you jumped on a cloud?
answer_in_one_line: You fall straight through: a small fair-weather cloud holds 500 tons of water (1.1 million pounds, a hundred elephants), but spread so thin that a fridge-sized piece holds ten drops; an 80 kg jumper is through it in 22 seconds and meets about one cup of water on the way.

why_this_one: The trend file offers no fresh row that passes all four tests, so this is the best unused tier A entry of the topic bank, from a cluster (sky) that neither of the last two episodes used (elevator, the snail). Everybody has looked out of a plane window or up from a lawn and wondered whether a cloud would hold him. The title is six plain words. A 6.3k-subscriber channel reached 927k views with the question, so it pulls without a big channel behind it. And the surprise is carried by numbers anyone can check: 0.5 grams of water per cubic metre (USGS) times a cubic kilometre is 500 tons, yet a fridge of it is ten drops and a whole fall through it is one cup. The mechanism (droplets so small that they sink half an inch a second) is carried by fog, a cloud that sat down. It is drawable with the kit: the garden, the open sky of an earlier episode, flat cards for the cloud, the balloon and the diagrams. Gus wears a parachute, lands on his own lawn and gets rained on; nobody is hurt and there is nothing a child could copy.
